title: Western Southampton: Deeds, Native Objections and Colonial Power
summary: Between Canoe Place and Seatuck, English settlers claimed land through overlapping agreements and a colonial governor’s ruling. Native people retained fishing and gathering rights, demanded continuing payments and challenged who had authority to sell. Westwoods remains Shinnecock land.
address_label: Western Southampton and barrier beaches — modern regional context
map_geometry_source: Modern regional coast added to the existing mainland outline. NYS boundaries and project shoreline; not a historic deed survey.
why_this_matters: A deed did not silence Native objections or erase every continuing right. Reading the agreements beside the protests and colonial rulings shows who asserted authority, what obligations remained, and why retained Shinnecock land must remain visible in the story.
introduction_title: Overlapping claims in a living Native homeland
introduction_content: Between Canoe Place and Seatuck, English settlers claimed land through overlapping agreements and a colonial governor’s ruling. Native people retained fishing and gathering rights, demanded continuing payments and challenged who had authority to sell. Westwoods remains Shinnecock land.
history_content:
A Native landscape between two bays

Western Southampton stretches from Canoe Place, at present-day Hampton Bays, toward Seatuck Creek at Eastport. To the north are the Peconic waters; to the south are the bays, creeks and beach landscapes around Quogue, Westhampton and Speonk. The colonial records describe an inhabited landscape through Native place names, meadows, fishing waters and access to coastal resources. They do not describe empty land waiting to be occupied. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

This chapter follows several overlapping claims rather than one moment when an entire region changed hands. Agreements involving English colonists Lion Gardiner, John Ogden and Thomas Topping recorded different interests and conditions. Native people negotiated, retained uses, challenged the authority of other signers and sought payment. Southampton's settler government then acquired papers and appealed to English colonial institutions to consolidate its claims. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

Grazing was not the same as giving up every coastal right

On June 10, 1658, Wyandance, his son Wiacombone and their associates made an agreement with Lion Gardiner concerning beach land west of Southampton's bounds. The document permitted grazing horses and cattle, required twenty-five shillings in annual rent, and reserved stranded whales to Native people. It also retained summer cutting of flags and bulrushes used to make mats, subject to a condition about not harming the horses. Different activities and obligations occupied the same landscape. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, p. 170

These clauses help explain why a land deed cannot automatically be read as a complete Native departure. The paper used hereditary transfer language while preserving particular Native relationships with the shore. Neither its wording nor its survival tells us that every affected person understood or accepted all its terms. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, p. 170

Ogden's agreement kept fishing, gathering and a recurring payment

The May 12, 1659 instrument names Wayandanch and his son Weuncombone with John Ogden. Its bounds refer to Southampton, Peconic waters and Potunck; the beach associated with John Cooper was excepted. It also preserved an existing meadow term for Thomas Halsey and his associates at Quaquantuck. The agreement expressly kept Native fishing, fowling and gathering of berries and other resources for their use. Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I, p. 156–157

The meadow arrangement included an annual twenty-five-shilling payment to Wayandanch or his heirs or assigns. On June 7, 1665, the colonial Court of Sessions at Southold ordered Southampton occupants to continue that payment to his daughter and heir, with recourse against Ogden. A later paper, dated January 17, 1670 as printed, records Thomas James claiming authority to accept eight trading-cloth coats and discharge the obligation. The sequence shows how continuing obligations could later become the subject of additional papers and claimed releases. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, p. 171–172

Topping's claim and the people who disputed it

On April 10, 1662, Weany Sunk Squaw, Anabackus and Jackanapes entered an agreement with Thomas Topping of Southampton. Other interested Native people also marked the instrument. It described land from Canoe Place, also called Niamuck, west to Seatuck and north toward the head of the bay. The stated payment was eighty fathoms of wampum or equivalent. The document also assigned half the profits from fish or whales cast upon the specified beach. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, p. 167–168

On September 17, 1666, another group of Native claimants expressly challenged the sellers' authority. Signers included Mandush's daughter and son, Quaquashaw, Punch and others. They said the earlier sellers had no right to make that conveyance and that the interest belonged principally to them. Their proposed assignment to Southampton was conditional: Governor Richard Nicolls was to determine whether they were the rightful proprietors and what payment should follow. This was an assertion of Native rights, not evidence that every Native person agreed to the earlier transaction. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, p. 169

An English governor decided among competing claims

Richard Nicolls governed the English colony of New York. His October 3, 1666 determination, issued at Fort James in New York, addressed competing claims involving Topping, John Cooper and Southampton's representatives John Howell and Henry Pierson. The order required papers and interests to be delivered to the town's purchasers and their successors, while treating whale profits separately. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, p. 172–174

Nicolls also directed payment of eighty fathoms of wampum or equivalent to the Native parties concerned. Distribution was left to the discretion of John Howell, Henry Pierson and Richard Howell. Naming these officials matters: colonial control grew through decisions about whose documents counted, who received interests and who decided compensation. A governor's order is evidence of that exercise of power; it is not an impartial resolution of all Native rights for all time. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, p. 173–174

The land history includes what the Nation kept

Westwoods must not be shown as simply lost because colonial papers claimed the surrounding region. In January 2025, the Shinnecock Nation announced that the U.S. Department of the Interior had reaffirmed Westwoods as continuously held restricted fee land. The Nation stated that the determination confirmed a status it had long maintained. This was recognition of retained land, not a new return of land and not permission for public access. Land Determination

LandBack and restoration belong alongside this history, but so does the defense of land never surrendered. Decisions about access, care and the future of Shinnecock land belong with the living Nation. Read this regional account together with West Woods, Shinnecock Indian Reservation and the histories of the communities and waterways within it. Land Determination

Continue with West Woods, Niamuck / Canoe Place, Quogue and Shinnecock Indian Reservation.

The beach was part of the relationship

The agreements described above concern more than mainland farms. The 1658 document distinguishes grazing from Native rights to stranded whales and summer gathering of flags and bulrushes. The 1659 agreement excepts a beach interest associated with John Cooper, while later records distinguish land claims from whale profits. Those differences show why the shore belongs in this story without treating every coastal right as a complete surrender. The modern barrier is shaded as a place to explore these records, not as an exact reconstruction of their changing beach boundaries. Southampton First Book, pp. 170 and 172–174; East Hampton Records, volume I, pp. 156–157
whereintheworld_content: This is a regional setting for overlapping records between Seatuck and Canoe Place, including modern western Southampton coastal islands and barrier beaches. It is not one deed boundary or a statement of current title. The modern canal helps locate Canoe Place but does not reconstruct the historic portage. Inlets, shores and engineered land have changed; the beach outline is not a claimed seventeenth-century inlet boundary. Westwoods remains excluded, and Shinnecock Indian Reservation remains outside this regional outline. Retained Native land is interpreted separately, not counted as land lost.
